instruction:
Step 1. Start from each `Invoice_Line_Items` record; combine it with each `Order_Items` record for which order item id (`Order_Items.order_item_id`) equals order item id (`Invoice_Line_Items.order_item_id`), one combined record per match (a record without a match is dropped); combine it with each `Orders` record for which order id (`Orders.order_id`) equals order id (`Order_Items.order_id`), one combined record per match (a record without a match is dropped); combine it with each `Customers` record for which customer id (`Customers.customer_id`) equals customer id (`Orders.customer_id`), one combined record per match (a record without a match is dropped); group the kept records by order item id (`Invoice_Line_Items.order_item_id`) and customer town or city (`Customers.town_city`); each group gives one result row; for each result row, return (1) order item id (`Invoice_Line_Items.order_item_id`); (2) customer town or city (`Customers.town_city`); (3) the average of product price per unit (`Invoice_Line_Items.product_price`) in the group (missing values ignored; missing when there are none); (4) the average of A ÷ B in the group (missing values ignored; missing when there are none). Here A is line product cost (`Invoice_Line_Items.derived_product_cost`); B is line total cost including VAT (`Invoice_Line_Items.derived_total_cost`).
Step 2. Start from the rows of step 1; group the kept records by column (2) of step 1; each group gives one result row; for each result row, return (1) column (2) of step 1; (2) the average of column (3) of step 1 in the group (missing values ignored; missing when there are none); (3) the average of column (4) of step 1 in the group (missing values ignored; missing when there are none).
Step 3. Start from the rows of step 2; all kept records form one group, which gives one result row; for each result row, return (1) the average of column (3) of step 2 in the group (missing values ignored; missing when there are none).
Step 4 (the answer). Start from the rows of step 2; combine it with the rows of step 3 for which it is not true that column (1) of step 3 is missing, one combined record per match (a record without a match is dropped); keep only the records for which column (3) of step 2 is greater than column (1) of step 3; for each kept record, return (1) column (1) of step 2; (2) column (2) of step 2; (3) column (3) of step 2; (4) A − B. Here A is column (3) of step 2; B is column (1) of step 3.
Conventions (SQLite's semantics): a condition that involves a missing value is undetermined, and neither it nor its negation holds. A formula is missing when any value in it is missing. Numbers are 64-bit integers or IEEE double-precision reals: ÷ is real-valued division (floating point); a division by 0 is missing; +, − and × of whole numbers stay whole unless the result leaves the 64-bit range, when it becomes a real; a sum of whole numbers that leaves that range is an error. a mod b is the remainder after both are truncated to whole numbers (missing when b truncates to 0). round rounds the double-precision value, halves away from zero; trunc truncates toward zero; text of a whole number is its decimal digits; sqrt, log10 and ln of a value outside their domain are missing; first_present is the first of its values that is not missing; nullif(a, b) is a, or missing when a equals b; larger and smaller are missing when any of their values is missing. Text is compared character by character, upper and lower case distinct (except in pattern matching). A date part of a value that is not a date is missing. When grouping or removing duplicates, missing values count as equal to each other.
reference_sql: WITH "s1" AS (SELECT "Invoice_Line_Items"."order_item_id" AS "e", "Customers"."town_city" AS "g", AVG("Invoice_Line_Items"."product_price") AS "m1", AVG((CAST("Invoice_Line_Items"."derived_product_cost" AS REAL) / "Invoice_Line_Items"."derived_total_cost")) AS "m2" FROM "Invoice_Line_Items" AS "Invoice_Line_Items" INNER JOIN "Order_Items" AS "Order_Items" ON "Order_Items"."order_item_id" = "Invoice_Line_Items"."order_item_id" INNER JOIN "Orders" AS "Orders" ON "Orders"."order_id" = "Order_Items"."order_id" INNER JOIN "Customers" AS "Customers" ON "Customers"."customer_id" = "Orders"."customer_id" GROUP BY "Invoice_Line_Items"."order_item_id", "Customers"."town_city"), "s2" AS (SELECT "s1"."g" AS "g", AVG("s1"."m1") AS "m1", AVG("s1"."m2") AS "m2" FROM "s1" AS "s1" GROUP BY "s1"."g"), "s3" AS (SELECT AVG("s2"."m2") AS "v" FROM "s2" AS "s2") SELECT "s2"."g" AS "g", "s2"."m1" AS "m1", "s2"."m2" AS "m2", ("s2"."m2" - "s3"."v") AS "m3" FROM "s2" AS "s2" INNER JOIN "s3" AS "s3" ON NOT ("s3"."v" IS NULL) WHERE "s2"."m2" > "s3"."v"

opus.meaning_reason: Each order item belongs to one order and so to one customer town, and the ratio of line product cost to total cost including VAT is a coherent share of the line total that is not VAT; the town averages and the difference from the mean over towns compare quantities of the same kind, and the instructions state the averaging-of-averages weighting.
opus.determined_reason: Every join, grouping, average, filter and output column is spelled out, so only one result is possible.
opus.interest_reason: Listing the towns whose average pre-VAT cost share is above the mean over towns, together with their average unit price, is coherent but of modest analytical value.

sonnet.meaning_reason: Every quantity has a coherent reading: m1 is the average unit price and m2 is the average pre-VAT cost share of the line total, each averaged per order item and then per town. The final column is the difference between a town's m2 and the equal-weighted mean of town m2 values, which are the same kind of quantity.
sonnet.determined_reason: The joins, groupings, averaging weights, filter and difference are all explicitly specified, so there is only one possible result.
sonnet.interest_reason: Comparing towns by cost share (pre-VAT cost over VAT-inclusive total) is coherent but mostly reflects VAT rates, so an analyst would have little reason to want it.
